text:
The American Bureau of Shipping (ABS), HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering (HD KSOE) and Siemens are working on a new digital twin system that could help predict how ammonia spreads on a ship after a leak.

The three companies signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to combine computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations with digital twin technology. The agreement was announced at Gastech 2026 in Bangkok.

The system will allow engineers to test different leak and accident situations during the ship design stage. This could help them find safety risks before construction starts.

The shipping industry is looking at ammonia as an alternative marine fuel as it tries to reduce its use of fossil fuels and cut emissions.

Green ammonia could significantly reduce the sector’s reliance on fossil fuels and lower emissions from shipping. But using ammonia as a marine fuel also comes with safety concerns.

Ammonia is highly corrosive and toxic if it is inhaled or comes into contact with the body. It can also catch fire at certain concentrations.

The project will look at what happens when ammonia leaks from a vessel and how the gas could spread.

Engineers will be able to test different leak and accident scenarios while the ship is still being designed. The aim is to better understand the risks before the vessel is built.

HD KSOE will work on ammonia safety systems and lead the related experimental research.

Siemens will provide the simulation and digital twin technology. ABS will provide a safety assessment method based on digital twins.

The project will bring together CFD simulations and digital twins to study ammonia leaks.

CFD can be used to model how ammonia spreads after a leak. The digital twin technology will then help engineers assess different leak and accident situations.

Chang Kwangpil, head of the Future Technology Institute at HD KSOE, said AI and digital twin technology could change the way research and development is carried out in shipbuilding.

He said the industry’s use of AI was not only about adopting new technology but also about changing how work is done. He added that AI and digital twins were expected to see greater use in shipbuilding research and development.

Byung Joon Oh, country manager of Siemens Digital Industries Software Korea, said physics-based simulation and digital twin technology could help improve the safety and engineering reliability of next-generation vessels.

He said the cooperation between Siemens, HD KSOE and ABS would help speed up safety checks for ammonia-fuelled vessels while supporting the wider use of digital technology in the marine industry.

The partnership will combine HD KSOE’s work on ammonia safety systems and experimental research with Siemens’ simulation and digital twin technology and ABS’ safety assessment method.

The companies said the technology could help engineers assess a wider range of ammonia leakage and accident scenarios early in the vessel design process.

title: World's First Hydrogen-Powered Coastal Tanker Completes Sea Trial in Japan
description:
A 4800 DWT coastal tanker, the Kikou Maru, successfully passed sea trials, in a world first for this configuration involving a four-stroke engine propelled by hydrogen, electric propulsion motors, and lithium-ion batteries to reduce fuel consumption.
In the engine trials, diesel oil was used to ignite a premix of hydrogen and air.
The tanker chosen for this test had to be designed for hydrogen propulsion; hence, Fukuoka Shipbuilding, a part of the project, chose the current one after it was launched in 2025.
The trial went on for two hours, during which the reported reduction in carbon dioxide emissions was 1.2 tons.
The trial produced extensive data regarding the adoption of hydrogen in coastal shipping and will be used as a benchmark to achieve efficiency in this direction.
text:
A 4800 DWT coastal tanker, the Kikou Maru, successfully passed sea trials, in a world first for this configuration involving a four-stroke engine propelled by hydrogen, electric propulsion motors, and lithium-ion batteries to reduce fuel consumption.

The engine was designed by Yanmar Power Solutions, and its first tests were conducted in 2024, during which it operated with an output of 500 kilowatts. In the engine trials, diesel oil was used to ignite a premix of hydrogen and air. Subsequent tests used hydrogenated vegetable oil for ignition.

The tanker chosen for this test had to be designed for hydrogen propulsion; hence, Fukuoka Shipbuilding, a part of the project, chose the current one after it was launched in 2025. The 105 m long tanker was finally sent to its owner, Uyeno TransTech.

The historic 20-mile-long sailing in Osaka Bay was part of a research program to support decarbonisation. The trial went on for two hours, during which the reported reduction in carbon dioxide emissions was 1.2 tons.

In this case, the engine produces electricity instead of just driving the propeller shafts, while electric motors provide propulsion through the two shafts.

Apart from testing the hydrogen engine on a tanker, the project includes research and development of a fuel supply system and a unique hull design to get AiP from ClassNK and also offer training and a usage manual for hydrogen-fuelled ships.

The trial produced extensive data regarding the adoption of hydrogen in coastal shipping and will be used as a benchmark to achieve efficiency in this direction.

Kazuma Kashiwagi, Director of the Environmental Bureau for Kobe, said that the trial is a vital step towards the application of hydrogen-fuelled vessels, generating zero emissions.

This could help decarbonise the shipping industry in Japan, which has set a goal of attaining carbon-neutrality in domestic shipping by 2050.

The project kicked off in 2022 and slowly progressed into different stages, including the development of a hydrogen fuel cell on an offshore vessel deployed to a wind farm, followed by a hydrogen engine for a tug.

All the tests, leading to this one, yielded important results and observations that helped achieve the next step in the development of a prototype engine for much larger vessels sailing the world’s oceans.

Apart from commercial cargo vessels, even cruise operators are testing fuel cells and hydrogen systems to produce electricity for operations in hotels and reduce port emissions.

text:
Moeve has closed an agreement with ISFA (Iberian Smart Financial Agro) to launch a pilot project for the use of 100% renewable diesel (HVO) with the aim of reducing emissions linked to the use of heavy agricultural machinery, according to both entities.

This trial program, with a planned duration of six months, is being carried out on a 600-hectare almond farm located in Logrosán (Cáceres) and will analyze the performance of this renewable fuel in various field tasks. HVO can be used in current engines and allows for a reduction of up to 90% in CO2 emissions over its entire life cycle compared to conventional diesel.

The trial, which started in June and will last approximately half a year, contemplates that Moeve will supply 15,000 liters of 100% renewable diesel, produced from organic waste, intended to fuel a fleet of 12 agricultural machines, consisting of eight tractors and four harvesters.

Currently, 28% of ISFA's carbon footprint comes from its agricultural machinery fleet. With this supply, the emission of 43 tons of CO2 will be avoided and the behavior of renewable fuels will be analyzed as a sustainable option that can be implemented immediately in sectors with complex electrification, such as heavy road transport, air traffic, and maritime transport.

The Commercial Director of the Clean Energies area of Moeve, Cristina Ballester, emphasized that reducing emissions linked to agricultural activity "is a priority to advance in the energy transition and requires immediate solutions that protect its competitiveness." "2G biofuels allow us to advance towards that goal with an already available alternative that is compatible with current engines," she said.

For his part, the partner and Sustainability Director of ISFA, Iker Baron, stressed that the introduction of 2G biofuels is "a great alternative to achieve our sustainability goals without the need to replace our machinery in the short term."

2G Biofuel Plant in Huelva to Ensure Supply

In order to guarantee the availability of 100% renewable diesel, Moeve is advancing together with its partner Apical in the construction of a new 2G biofuel plant in Huelva, which will be integrated into the largest second-generation renewable fuel complex in southern Europe.

The project adds up to a cumulative investment of 1.200 million euros and will have a flexible production capacity of 500,000 tons annually of HVO and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). This facility will be decisive to meet the company's goal of leading the Iberian market of 2G biofuels, with a production of 2.5 million tons per year by 2030.

title: EU Taxonomy: General Court largely upholds aviation and shipping criteria
authors: Julia Voskoboinikova, Julia Grothaus, Daniella Strik, Guillaume Croisant
description:
On 30 September 2026, the EU General Court ruled on a challenge brought by three environmental NGOs against the technical screening criteria for aviation and maritime transport under the EU Taxonomy, adopted by the European Commission in 2023.
The NGOs had asked the Commission to withdraw the criteria allowing certain conventional aircraft and gas-fuelled vessels to count as "transitional" sustainable activities.
The Taxonomy criteria for aviation and shipping remain in force and continue to apply.
In practice, however, the methane-slippage condition for gas-fuelled vessels should now be read subject to the Court's finding.
The Commission must re-open the internal review on that point and is expected to revise the maritime criteria.
text:
On 30 September 2026, the EU General Court ruled on a challenge brought by three environmental NGOs against the technical screening criteria for aviation and maritime transport under the EU Taxonomy, adopted by the European Commission in 2023.

The NGOs had asked the Commission to withdraw the criteria allowing certain conventional aircraft and gas-fuelled vessels to count as "transitional" sustainable activities. The Commission refused in June 2024. The NGOs took the refusal to the EU General Court. For more information, see our previous blog post. The Court dismissed almost the entire action. It confirmed the Commission's broad discretion under Article 19 of the Taxonomy Regulation. It rejected both aviation pleas, including challenges to the CO2 thresholds, the fleet replacement ratio and the minimum sustainable aviation fuel percentages. It also rejected most of the maritime pleas.

The Court upheld one point of the challenge: for gas-fuelled vessels, a requirement to use "state-of-the-art" methane-slippage mitigation cannot stand on its own. Where verification depends on compliance with emissions thresholds, the criterion must either set those thresholds itself or expressly cross-refer to an identifiable standard (such as FuelEU Maritime). On that basis, the Commission's refusal to re-examine the criteria was annulled to that limited extent.

The Taxonomy criteria for aviation and shipping remain in force and continue to apply. In practice, however, the methane-slippage condition for gas-fuelled vessels should now be read subject to the Court's finding. The Commission must re-open the internal review on that point and is expected to revise the maritime criteria. The timing has not been announced, and an appeal to the Court of Justice on points of law remains open to either side.

text:
FuelEU Maritime remains one of the shipping industry’s biggest decarbonisation drivers, with 2026 marking a critical year for compliance.

FuelEU Maritime came into force on 1 January 2025 with the aim of increasing the uptake of zero and low carbon fuels. It does so by setting incremental targets for the reduction of greenhouse gas (GHG) intensity of onboard energy, covering both fuels and electricity, on voyages involving EU ports. The reduction target started at 2% in 2025 and will go up to 6% by 2030, ultimately reaching 80% by 2050.

This year alone, there are three key milestones to mark in calendars.

By 31 March, verified results are confirmed and indicate each vessel’s compliance surplus or deficit. The period between this checkpoint and the next is crucial as companies have a short window to improve their position before any remaining deficit leads to penalties in the summer.

By 30 April, companies must decide on their compliance strategy if they are in a deficit. The main options are borrowing or pooling. Borrowing offers some flexibility but is limited to cases where the GHG intensity gap does not exceed2%.

By May – June, penalties for non-compliance will be applied.

Each compliance strategy has its strengths and choosing between the two is far from a matter of preference. Operators will need to choose the strategy that aligns best with their operational priorities.

Between borrowing and pooling, there are key differences:

Borrowing can only be applied where the GHG intensity shortfall is no greater than 2%.

There is a 10% penalty applied to borrowed surplus next year.

Cannot be used in two consecutive years.

Pooling can offset your deficit using the surplus from other vessels

No penalty multiplier offering an easier path to compliance

Can be applied across an entire fleet

Ultimately, the optimal approach depends on each fleet’s exposure and trading profile. What is clear, however, is that penalties are avoidable with the right preparation.

A robust compliance strategy starts with understanding your exposure. Not just in general terms, but on a voyage by voyage and trade by trade basis. That foundation is what allows operators to assess the financial, carbon and compliance consequences in real terms, and to act before options become limited. With continued market volatility, flexibility, speed of execution and proactivity matter. Pooling and other mechanisms work best when deployed early – not at the deadline.

At KPI OceanConnect, we help simplify this complexity. Our dedicated Alternative Fuels & Carbon Markets team of experts can guide our partners every step of the way in understanding the best options available and what makes sense operationally and commercially. We support our customers with access to pooling solutions through partnerships with two highly reputable pooling providers, combining compliance expertise with practical execution capabilities. We connect you to the right pool, optimise your fuel position with tailored recommendations that work alongside your compliance balance, and handle your EUA procurement, all managed through one partner.

Demand Drivers in the Market

Fleet operators need reliable engine and propeller control. Small control errors can increase fuel use and affect ship handling.

Hybrid ships need controls that manage engine and electric power together. This keeps thrust steady when batteries and engines share the load.

Shipyards need control units that work with diesel shaft and diesel-electric systems. Clear start-up steps make ship approval easier.

Control system companies should use common marine connections. This makes it easier to connect engines and gearboxes across different vessels.

Engine control manages engine speed and power from the bridge. Gear and clutch control connects the engine to the shaft at the right time. Propeller pitch control changes the propeller angle. Hybrid drive control manages batteries, electric drives, and other power sources.

Fleet ships are forecast to account for 29.0% share in 2026.

Commercial ships need control system replacements during their service life. Naval vessels need reliable backup systems. Offshore vessels need steady thrust to stay in position, while ferries need good control at low speeds. Yachts and workboats need small control units that are easy to use.

Diesel shaft is forecast to lead with 36.0% share in 2026.

Diesel shaft systems are widely used because one unit controls the engine, gearbox, and thrust. Diesel-electric systems also control generators and motors. This Report Answers

The report explains how propulsion control units connect bridge commands with engines and propellers across conventional and electrified vessel architectures.

Segment analysis identifies the leading subsegments and explains why control requirements differ across vessel types and propulsion layouts.

Country analysis compares five markets and the operating conditions that shape propulsion-control demand.

Competitive analysis reviews active suppliers by control products and integration breadth without adding company market-share estimates.

What does the Marine Propulsion Control Units Market cover?

The Marine Propulsion Control Units Market covers hardware and software that command vessel propulsion and coordinate response with bridge inputs. Related marine steering systems influence maneuvering but remain outside the core propulsion-control boundary.

The assessment includes interfaces with marine switchboards when ship power affects propulsion operation. The switchboard itself remains a separate equipment category.

The core test for scope is whether the product sends or shapes a propulsion command. A display that only shows data stays outside the core category. A unit that checks a bridge order and sends a safe engine or propeller command stays inside. This rule keeps the market focused on command and control while still allowing links with power and ship automation systems.

What is included in the scope?

Included offerings cover propulsion-control hardware and operator interfaces that directly command engines or propellers. The scope can interact with marine gensets when generator loading affects diesel-electric propulsion response.

The analysis includes coordination with marine power battery systems where stored energy limits influence hybrid or fully electric propulsion commands.

Shaft-driven power functions are considered when they affect propulsion coordination, including interaction with marine shaft generator systems in integrated powertrains.

What is excluded from the scope?

Standalone engines and turbocharging hardware fall outside the control-unit boundary. Adjacent marine turbochargers are treated as engine components unless their actuators are directly managed by the propulsion controller.

Fuel supply remains outside the market boundary, including low-carbon ammonia propulsion as a fuel category. Control units that manage engine response to alternative-fuel operation remain within scope.

title: S-100 and the Connected Bridge: In Conversation with Stephan Dimke of Teledyne ...
description:
Following the strategic unification of ChartWorld and Raymarine Commercial earlier this year, the maritime industry has gained a powerful new entity in digital bridge solutions: Teledyne Raymarine Commercial.
To dive deeper into what this integration means for the future of maritime operations, Adonis Violaris of CSN sat down with Stephan Dimke, General Manager of Teledyne Raymarine Commercial.
Earlier this year we saw the strategic unification of ChartWorld and Raymarine Commercial under a single global navigation brand.
The unification of ChartWorld and Raymarine Commercial under one global navigation brand – Teledyne Raymarine Commercial – isn’t only a brand name change; it’s a reaction to how the commercial maritime navigation market is altering, in particular the shift to S-100 navigational standards.
At Teledyne Raymarine Commercial, we are committed to investing in the people and processes that will determine whether the system’s potential is realised.
text:
Following the strategic unification of ChartWorld and Raymarine Commercial earlier this year, the maritime industry has gained a powerful new entity in digital bridge solutions: Teledyne Raymarine Commercial. This merger seamlessly blends software-driven digital solutions with robust marine hardware, offering shipowners a single, cohesive partner for their bridge requirements.

To dive deeper into what this integration means for the future of maritime operations, Adonis Violaris of CSN sat down with Stephan Dimke, General Manager of Teledyne Raymarine Commercial. With the impending transition to S-100 standards, the growing need for maritime cybersecurity, and the ongoing push for decarbonisation, bridge teams face an increasingly complex operating environment.

In this exclusive Q&A, Dimke shares his insights on how the new Pathfinder ECDIS simplifies chart management, the evolution of the “ECDIS as a Service” model, and the tangible benefits of solid-state radar technology for modern fleets.

Earlier this year we saw the strategic unification of ChartWorld and Raymarine Commercial under a single global navigation brand. This brings together software-driven digital navigation and robust marine hardware into one cohesive organisation. How has this integration progressed so far, and what are the main synergies visitors will see at your stand during SMM Hamburg?

The unification of ChartWorld and Raymarine Commercial under one global navigation brand – Teledyne Raymarine Commercial – isn’t only a brand name change; it’s a reaction to how the commercial maritime navigation market is altering, in particular the shift to S-100 navigational standards. Software-driven digital navigation and marine hardware have historically sat separately, often with different vendors, contracts, and support lines. Bringing them together means a shipowner now has one accountable partner across the full navigation stack: charts and data, ECDIS and hardware, and the service and support model that ties them together.

We were able to demonstrate some of our navigation tools at this year’s SMM Hamburg – like our Pathfinder ECDIS running live alongside our radar and bridge hardware. We demonstrated the navigation ecosystem as one cohesive system rather than a collection of separate products – a preview of exactly how S-100 can optimise data usage for navigation.

The transition to the new S-100 universal hydrographic data model is a major focal point for the shipping industry right now. Your recently launched Pathfinder ECDIS was specifically designed to support this next-generation ENC standard. Can you walk us through how this new system simplifies chart installation and what shipowners need to know to ensure a smooth transition?

Ultimately, S-100 changes what ‘chart installation’ even means – for example, under S-57, installing charts is a manual task: you load a subscription and apply the updates. S-100 replaces that static, single-source picture with continuously updated, multi-layered data: bathymetry, water levels, surface currents, navigational warnings, each on its own update cycle.

Pathfinder ECDIS was designed for that world as an S-100-ready system built to run the new data layers as they mature, not a slicker or ‘updated’ version of the old model. The point isn’t a one-off installation; it’s taking the manual update burden off the bridge, so the vessel is always working from current data without the crew managing that by hand.

S-100-capable ECDIS has been permitted since January 2026, and starting in January 2029, every new installation and retrofit must meet the standard. However, type-approved S-100 ECDIS aren’t expected to be commercially available until around 2028, so no one is operating a finished, type-approved S-100 system today. In the meantime, S-57 and S-100 run side by side in dual-fuel mode, with no withdrawal date set for the older standard — both will be supported for the foreseeable future. That overlap could pose real risk as bridge teams work with two data standards at once, with genuine potential for confusion in critical moments during a voyage.

So a smooth transition turns less on the box on the bridge and more on the decisions around it. Which data layers are mandatory for a given voyage? Whose call is it when bridge and shore read the same dataset and reach different conclusions? How are officers trained and supported through the first months of live operation? This is why we talk about subscribing to be ready rather than rushing to install: a managed, service-based model lets a fleet get onto the transition path now, prepare its people and processes on its own timescale, and switch fully to S-100 when the moment is right — rather than working it all out in real time once dual-fuel operation begins. The system matters, but mainly because it buys the runway to get the people and processes right, and that’s where the safety and efficiency gains are realised or lost.

Bridge teams today face an unprecedented amount of data, which can often lead to cognitive overload during critical watchkeeping duties. Raymarine has traditionally focused on intuitive, user-friendly interfaces to mitigate this issue. How are your latest integrated bridge solutions engineered to reduce this burden and minimise the need for extensive crew training?

The change is not simply more data; it is data of a different kind: dynamic, time-dependent data that is continuously updated. This creates a system incorporating layers of information for crews on the bridge, providing a universal standard, allowing for real-time updates, and enabling access to route optimisation that can vastly improve environmental performance and commercial efficiency simultaneously.

For bridge crews, the training processes and support during the transitional phase will be key to ensuring smooth implementation. Officers will need to focus more on interpreting system outputs, validating recommendations, and maintaining situational awareness, rather than manually processing raw navigational data. At Teledyne Raymarine Commercial, we are committed to investing in the people and processes that will determine whether the system’s potential is realised.

You personally pioneered the “ECDIS as a Service” concept back in 2011, which shifted the industry from viewing navigation as a hardware purchase to a subscription-based platform. Now, under the unified Teledyne Raymarine Commercial umbrella, how is this subscription-based navigation model evolving to meet the cost efficiency and operational demands of modern fleet managers?

With S-100, AI and hardware platforms that develop this quickly, an as-a-Service model makes more sense than ever. Nobody can say today which processor will be needed in five years to run the software that future navigation systems require. Shipowners who want a predictable budget for their bridge equipment and the lowest possible lifetime cost for their navigation systems will find it hard to avoid a service-based approach.

With vessels becoming increasingly connected to shore-based infrastructure, maritime cybersecurity is no longer optional. We note that systems like the Pathfinder ECDIS utilise an embedded operating system and the eSync onboard gateway. How do these architectural choices actively protect the vessel’s navigational network from external cyber threats and ensure compliance with international cybersecurity standards?

One of the fundamental changes S-100 will trigger is the shore-based team having access to the same operational data the bridge is working with, in near real time. This development is unprecedented in terms of optimising the relationship between the office and the vessel for safer and more efficient fleet operations. For cybersecurity standards, for example, not only will the data be equipped to incorporate up-to-date security intelligence, but the embedded operating system – which is fundamental to the Pathfinder ECDIS – also reduces exposure from uncontrolled external connectivity.

Environmental compliance and decarbonisation are dominating boardroom discussions across the maritime sector. While much of the focus is on alternative fuels, voyage optimisation plays an equally critical role in immediate fuel savings. How do your connected voyage planning tools and navigation data services directly support shipowners in reducing their carbon footprint?

Fuel costs, particularly in recent months, will be a hot topic for shipowner and operator boardroom conversations, while shipping’s energy transition will play out over many years. What fuel costs today and longer-term decarbonisation share is that voyage optimisation is paramount; fuel costs are high, and will only become incrementally higher with new, alternative fuels.

Our connected planning tools draw on live weather, current, and tidal data to determine the routing and speed profile that consumes the least fuel, and the available independent evidence is consistent. The IMO itself estimates weather routing fuel savings at between three per cent and 10%, depending on ship type.

With the IMO’s global Net-Zero Framework adoption postponed last October, the rules that apply today are regional. The EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime both price emissions per tonne and impose a cost. Every tonne of fuel a better route avoids is a tonne you don’t buy an ETS allowance for, a lighter FuelEU penalty, and a stronger carbon-intensity rating for the vessel. And because carbon intensity is measured per tonne-mile, carrying more cargo on the same optimised voyage improves the number twice over.

The dynamic layers S-100 introduces, i.e., near-real-time surface currents and hour-by-hour water levels, are precisely the inputs route optimisation depends on, and the next phase of the standard is focused specifically on route planning. As a result, the picture a planning tool works from becomes far richer and more current than static charts ever allowed. However, type-approved S-100 systems aren’t expected on the market until around 2028, and the gains from this will depend on training and workflow changes alongside the technology.

Radar technology is foundational to situational awareness, yet we still see many fleets relying on legacy magnetron systems. Raymarine has been disrupting this space with the IMO-compliant Pathfinder solid-state X-band radar. What are the tangible operational benefits of moving to solid-state technology regarding hazard detection, maintenance reduction, and overall vessel safety?

A solid-state radar changes things for everyone who deals with it, starting with the mariner. Because the transmitter is phase-locked, it is optimally tuned for every pulse, so the operator no longer has to re-tune it. Coherent signal processing detects small targets in clutter better and improves the automatic clutter algorithms. The radar also checks its own performance and alerts the crew, which removes the need for manual records. And because a solid-state transmitter keeps its detection capability over time, operators can rely on what they see on the screen.

For the maintainer, built-in test equipment finds errors quickly without major teardowns. A quick-install cabling kit and a lightweight design make installation and repairs simpler.

For owners and operators, it comes down to cost. A magnetron typically needs replacing every year, and that often leads to unplanned and expensive repairs. Our Pathfinder solid-state radar avoids these frequent service needs and the damage that can come with them. That lowers service costs and makes it more cost-effective over its lifetime.

Looking beyond current compliance cycles, the maritime industry is steadily moving towards highly automated and data-driven operating environments. With the combined expertise of ChartWorld, SevenCs, and Raymarine now at your disposal, what major technological shifts do you foresee in commercial navigation over the next three to five years, and how are you preparing your clients for that future?

We do see guided navigation. As the data available for decision-making grows and updates become more frequent, the navigator on board will focus on supervising decision suggestions. Day-to-day voyage planning will become less important and take less time. The winning skill set in the future will be the ability to act on a situation picture, including fused sensor data and automatically generated voyage plans.

0

APM Terminals Nigeria has called for stronger collaboration among government, industry, investors and development partners to accelerate the development of bankable green infrastructure projects capable of transforming Nigeria’s maritime sector and supporting the country’s transition to a low-carbon economy.

The call was made by APM Terminals Nigeria Chairman, Frederik Klinke, at the second Decarbonizing Infrastructure in Nigeria (DIN) Summit in Abuja, themed “De-risking Green Infrastructure Investments: From Policy Architecture to Bankable Projects.”

Addressing policymakers, industry leaders and development partners, Klinke said Nigeria has made significant progress in advancing maritime reforms and climate action but stressed that the next phase must focus on implementation.

“Policy alone does not reduce emissions. Strategies do not decarbonize ports. Frameworks do not attract investment. Projects do,” he said.

Klinke emphasized the need to translate policy ambition into scalable, investment-ready projects that deliver both economic and environmental benefits.

Noting that maritime transport accounts for more than 80 per cent of global trade by volume, he said decarbonising the sector is critical to achieving climate goals and strengthening long-term economic competitiveness. He highlighted the importance of regulatory clarity, project readiness, reliable emissions data, and stronger integration across ports, roads, rail and inland logistics networks.

Also speaking at the summit, CEO of APM Terminals Nigeria, Koen De Backker, highlighted the critical role of ports and terminals in the energy transition, noting that reducing emissions begins with improving the efficiency of logistics systems. He said this can be achieved by reducing equipment usage and fuel consumption, minimising truck waiting times and congestion, improving cargo flow and operational efficiency, supporting cleaner energy solutions, and preparing for the adoption of lower-emission technologies.

“Maritime decarbonization is not only a fuels challenge. It is also an operational challenge,” De Backker said.

Representing Vice President Kashim Shettima, Deputy Chief of Staff Senator Ibrahim Hadejia called for urgent policy reforms, stronger public-private partnerships and innovative risk-sharing mechanisms to attract domestic and foreign investment into Nigeria’s green infrastructure sector. He said achieving Nigeria’s climate and infrastructure objectives would require greater participation from the private sector, development finance institutions and institutional investors, supported by well-prepared projects capable of attracting long-term capital.

Personal Assistant to the President on Subnational Infrastructure and representative of the DIN Summit Steering Committee, Musaddiq Adamu, said the summit was established to address a critical challenge: moving green infrastructure projects from concept to investment. He noted that engagements from previous editions had already produced tangible outcomes, including progress on port electrification initiatives. According to Adamu, discussions following APM Terminals’ presentation at the inaugural summit contributed to a partnership with the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA) aimed at advancing the electrification of port operations and positioning Onne Port as a leading example of green port development in Nigeria.

Klinke had earlier highlighted APM Terminals Nigeria’s contribution to the country’s decarbonisation agenda, including the launch of a white paper outlining practical pathways for reducing emissions across Nigeria’s container logistics value chain. The report demonstrates how electrification of logistics operations can stimulate investment, improve energy reliability, create skilled jobs, enhance public health outcomes and reduce supply chain emissions.

As part of its long-term commitment to sustainable logistics, APM Terminals, in partnership with the NPA, plans to invest in green power infrastructure and electric equipment across its Apapa and Onne operations. The initiative is expected to strengthen Nigeria’s trade competitiveness while advancing the country’s climate ambitions.

“The question before us is no longer whether decarbonisation will happen. The question is whether we will create the partnerships, frameworks and investment environment needed to make it happen at the pace required,” Klinke said.

He urged stakeholders to move beyond dialogue and focus on execution, noting that the infrastructure investments and partnerships established today will help shape Nigeria’s future economy, trade competitiveness and environmental sustainability.

text:
Hello Readers,

There is a strong move by India’s top container ports such Jawaharlal Nehru Port, Chennai Port and Mundra Port to set up empty container depots either by themselves or through a Public-Private-Partnership (PPP) model.

The strategy appears to be to streamline this intrinsic part of the container logistics ecosystem, a business which was hitherto the preserve of landowners or those looking to utilise leased land or encroached land to support India’s export-import trade through a cozy understanding with the shipping lines.

The game plan is also aimed at infusing transparency in the rates levied by the empty container park operators, at least in the case of state-owned ports such as Jawaharlal Nehru Port and Chennai Port.

Advt

The empty container yard operators have been an unregulated business so far, raising concerns from the EXIM trade, particularly exporters, who are dependent on these empty boxes to stuff cargo for exports. Since pandemic times, equipment availability has been a major grouse of exporters, forcing the government to intervene.

Streamlining the activity would also help improve the operating environment of transporters and driver communities.

This is our main story for the week.

Read the story here.

Other Top Stories

Deendayal Port bets on private capital for green fuel push

State-owned Deendayal Port Authority (Kandla Port) is tapping potential for green fuel bunkering by setting up facilities with private funds. The port authority had previously leased land to private green fuel producers to develop facilities by leveraging its land and waterfront.

The latest initiative involving private firms is yet another step in this direction. The move gels with the government’s plan to make India a major green fuel producer as the global shipping industry slowly pivots towards green fuels for running ships in line with the initiatives taken by the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) to cut emissions.

Deendayal Port Authority’s plan is explained in this article. Read here.

APSEZ doubles Colombo terminal capacity to 3.2 million TEUs

Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Ltd (APSEZ), India’s biggest private port operator, has bolstered its container transhipment play in the Indian Ocean region by raising the capacity of its West Container Terminal in Colombo Port to 3.2 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) from 1.6 million TEUs a year with an investment of some $750 million.

Advt

With the capacity enhancement, APSEZ is on course to meet its ambition of handling some 25 per cent of Colombo Port’s targeted capacity of 13 million TEUs by 2028.

The West Container Terminal has already handled some 2 million TEUs in just 18 months of starting the first phase.

In the same region, APSEZ is increasing the capacity of its container transhipment port at Vizhinjam in Kerala to handle 5.7 million TEUs from 1 million TEUs a year. Read here.

Four Indian ports get ‘mega port’ status

India’s ports received a shot in the arm with the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways designating four ports as mega ports based on a volume matrix.

But, unlike Central Public Sector Undertakings that are graded maharatna, navratna and mini ratna, as the case maybe, with attendant financial powers to take decisions, the mega port status does not appear to come with any special powers and privileges.

Yet, it’s a designation that can be flaunted by the ports to leverage its standing in the shipping industry while dealing with ship owners and other key stakeholders to grow the port and improve their standing.

It is also an incentive for those who are yet to get that status to strive to reach the goalpost. Read here.

Priya Blue becomes target of online fake news campaign

This is a hit job by mischief makers, ostensibly at the behest of ‘rivals’ in the industry who don’t have the magnanimity to see others grow.

Ship recycling is a tough business with the constant glare of regulators, environmental groups, NGOs etc. On top of this, Priya Blue Industries, India’s biggest ship recycler by number of vessels and tonnage dismantled, became the target of a concerted attempt by rogue websites to malign reputation and stall business prospects.

ETInfra stumbled upon the story that exposes the dangers facing business groups in a digital world that is evolving at lightening speed with new tactics being deployed by fraudsters to cause reputational harm, leaving those affected clueless about what to do. Read here.

Mundra empty-container strike ends after month-long standoff

The final pick of the week– that just went by– again, is a story on empty container yards.

After a month-long impasse, Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Ltd and the empty box depot operators at Mundra Port arrived at a settlement to end the strike triggered by APSEZ’s move to alter the system of handling empty containers at India’s busiest container gateway located in Gujarat.

It was one of the rare occasions when APSEZ was forced to reverse its stand, mainly due to the Gujarat government’s involvement, before the situation spun out of control for India’s export-import trade, with global attention riveted on the issue given Mundra’s status.

The details of the settlement have been captured in this story. Read here.

That’s all for this week!

From ports seeking greater control over empty-container operations to investments in green-fuel infrastructure and expanding container capacity across the Indian Ocean, the week highlighted how India’s ports are looking to strengthen both the efficiency and competitiveness of the wider maritime ecosystem.

Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Ltd (APSEZ), India’s biggest private port operator, has bolstered its container transhipment play in the Indian Ocean region by raising the capacity of its West Container Terminal in Colombo Port to 3.2 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) from 1.6 million TEUs a year with an investment of some $750 million.

With the capacity enhancement, APSEZ is on course to meet its ambition of handling some 25 per cent of Colombo Port’s targeted capacity of 13 million TEUs by 2028.

The West Container Terminal has already handled some 2 million TEUs in just 18 months of starting the first phase.

In the same region, APSEZ is increasing the capacity of its container transhipment port at Vizhinjam in Kerala to handle 5.7 million TEUs from 1 million TEUs a year. Read here.

Four Indian ports get ‘mega port’ status

India’s ports received a shot in the arm with the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways designating four ports as mega ports based on a volume matrix.

But, unlike Central Public Sector Undertakings that are graded maharatna, navratna and mini ratna, as the case maybe, with attendant financial powers to take decisions, the mega port status does not appear to come with any special powers and privileges.

Yet, it’s a designation that can be flaunted by the ports to leverage its standing in the shipping industry while dealing with ship owners and other key stakeholders to grow the port and improve their standing.

It is also an incentive for those who are yet to get that status to strive to reach the goalpost. Read here.

Priya Blue becomes target of online fake news campaign

This is a hit job by mischief makers, ostensibly at the behest of ‘rivals’ in the industry who don’t have the magnanimity to see others grow.

Ship recycling is a tough business with the constant glare of regulators, environmental groups, NGOs etc. On top of this, Priya Blue Industries, India’s biggest ship recycler by number of vessels and tonnage dismantled, became the target of a concerted attempt by rogue websites to malign reputation and stall business prospects.

ETInfra stumbled upon the story that exposes the dangers facing business groups in a digital world that is evolving at lightening speed with new tactics being deployed by fraudsters to cause reputational harm, leaving those affected clueless about what to do. Read here.

Mundra empty-container strike ends after month-long standoff

The final pick of the week– that just went by– again, is a story on empty container yards.

After a month-long impasse, Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Ltd and the empty box depot operators at Mundra Port arrived at a settlement to end the strike triggered by APSEZ’s move to alter the system of handling empty containers at India’s busiest container gateway located in Gujarat.

It was one of the rare occasions when APSEZ was forced to reverse its stand, mainly due to the Gujarat government’s involvement, before the situation spun out of control for India’s export-import trade, with global attention riveted on the issue given Mundra’s status.

The details of the settlement have been captured in this story. Read here.

From ports seeking greater control over empty-container operations to investments in green-fuel infrastructure and expanding container capacity across the Indian Ocean, the week highlighted how India’s ports are looking to strengthen both the efficiency and competitiveness of the wider maritime ecosystem.

title: Vehicle importers, shippers demand review of new GSA PVoC regime | 3News
description: The stakeholders are demanding broader consultations with industry players, arguing that implementation of the new regime could have significant implications for vehicle importation and businesses operating within the automotive trade.
text:
Members of the Vehicle Import Dealers Association of Ghana, shippers and freight forwarders are calling on the Ghana Standards Authority (GSA) to suspend or reconsider the mandatory Pre-Export Verification of Conformity (PVoC) programme for imported vehicles.

The stakeholders are demanding broader consultations with industry players, arguing that implementation of the new regime could have significant implications for vehicle importation and businesses operating within the automotive trade.

The PVoC programme, which took effect on October 1, 2026, requires used vehicles destined for Ghana to undergo conformity verification before shipment from the country of origin. The process is intended to ensure that vehicles comply with applicable Ghanaian standards, including GS 4510.

The GSA has said the programme is aimed at improving road safety, protecting consumers and preventing non-conforming vehicles from entering the Ghanaian market.

However, vehicle importers, shippers and freight forwarders say they have concerns about the manner in which the policy is being implemented.

The stakeholders are proposing an alternative arrangement under which imported used and salvaged vehicles would be inspected by the Ghana Standards Authority at Ghana's ports of entry.

They want the Parliamentary Select Committee on Trade, Industry and Tourism to engage the GSA on the policy and impress upon the Authority to consider the proposed port-based inspection system.

According to industry players, inspections at the ports would enable the GSA to directly assess vehicles arriving in Ghana while creating an opportunity for closer engagement between the regulator, importers, shippers and other stakeholders.

The groups maintain that their concerns are not against vehicle safety or conformity standards, but rather the timing, process and implementation of the mandatory pre-shipment inspection requirement.

The concerns are also being raised by some vehicle shippers operating in the United States, where vehicles destined for Ghana must now meet the conformity requirements before shipment.

Some U.S.-based shipping operators say the new requirements have created uncertainty for vehicles being prepared for export to Ghana, particularly where the required conformity verification has not been completed.

The change is significant because the inspection requirement moves an important part of the compliance process from Ghana's ports to the country of origin.

Industry players say this could affect the ability of some exporters and shipping companies to load vehicles for Ghana until the necessary conformity requirements have been satisfied.

The new regime has therefore become a concern for businesses involved in the Ghana-U.S. vehicle trade, with stakeholders calling for clearer procedures and greater engagement between the GSA and industry.

The Vehicle Import Dealers Association of Ghana has also raised concerns about the potential impact of the policy on the volume of vehicles imported into the country and the wider automotive trade.

The association argues that if the policy is not carefully reviewed, some businesses could face difficulties in continuing their operations.

The stakeholders are consequently calling for a system that protects consumers and ensures compliance with safety standards while taking into account the operational realities of importers, freight forwarders and international vehicle shippers.

They are also seeking greater clarity on the inspection process, certification requirements and how the programme will be implemented across different vehicle-exporting countries.

The Ghana Standards Authority maintains that the PVoC programme is intended to ensure that vehicles imported into Ghana meet the country's applicable standards before they are shipped.

Under the programme, used vehicles destined for Ghana are required to demonstrate conformity with the applicable requirements through the prescribed verification and certification process.

The GSA's position is that the system will help prevent non-conforming vehicles from entering the country and strengthen consumer protection.

The Authority has also worked with designated inspection partners to commence pre-shipment inspections and the issuance of Certificates of Conformity for vehicles exported to Ghana.

Despite the GSA's position, industry stakeholders want further consultations before the new system is fully entrenched.

They are urging Parliament, the GSA and other relevant authorities to engage vehicle importers, dealers, shippers and freight forwarders to address concerns surrounding the programme.

The stakeholders say their objective is not to undermine vehicle safety standards, but to ensure that the conformity assessment regime is practical, transparent and does not unnecessarily disrupt the vehicle importation and shipping industry.

For now, the industry is calling for continued dialogue on the PVoC programme and consideration of a system that balances vehicle safety and regulatory compliance with the concerns of businesses involved in the importation and shipment of vehicles to Ghana.

title: First US' ship-to-ship ethanol bunkering of deep-sea vessel completed - Interesting Engineering
description:
This operation provided valuable insight into the operational, infrastructure, sourcing and supply chain considerations for using ethanol as a marine fuel.
This bunkering operation aboard Tangier Maersk provides valuable real-world experience with alternative fuels in commercial shipping.
Corn is one of the principal feedstocks for U.S. ethanol production, meaning greater use of ethanol in shipping could potentially create another market for American biofuel producers.
The use of U.S.-produced corn ethanol also highlights the increasingly interconnected nature of the energy, agricultural and maritime sectors.
The U.S. is already a major global ethanol producer, with an established network of production facilities and distribution infrastructure.
text:
Operation builds on previous ethanol trials

“The operation builds on previous ethanol trials aboard Laura Maersk and Antonia Maersk and reflects Maersk’s continued commitment to exploring and advancing credible pathways to drive progress within the shipping industry’s energy transition,” said Ditlev Blicher, Maersk Regional President for North America.

This operation provided valuable insight into the operational, infrastructure, sourcing and supply chain considerations for using ethanol as a marine fuel. While ethanol benefits from an established production base, existing infrastructure and compatibility with alcohol-enabled vessel technology, scalable future fuel pathways will also depend on fuel availability, regulation and operational readiness across the maritime value chain, according to a press release.

Real-world experience with alternative fuels in commercial shipping

Achieving lower-emission logistics requires turning new technologies into practical, scalable solutions. This bunkering operation aboard Tangier Maersk provides valuable real-world experience with alternative fuels in commercial shipping. The insights gained will help drive the development of more sustainable supply chains, as per the release.

The development is notable because ethanol already has a large-established production and distribution network in the United States. Using an existing fuel supply chain could potentially provide an advantage as shipping companies investigate alternatives to conventional fossil-based marine fuels.

The operation also creates a connection between the U.S. agricultural sector and the global maritime industry. Corn is one of the principal feedstocks for U.S. ethanol production, meaning greater use of ethanol in shipping could potentially create another market for American biofuel producers.

Tangier Maersk is equipped with alcohol-enabled dual-fuel propulsion

The Tangier Maersk is equipped with an alcohol-enabled dual-fuel propulsion system, allowing the vessel to operate using alternative alcohol-based fuels alongside conventional marine fuel. Industry reporting has described the vessel as a roughly 9,000-TEU container ship measuring about 270 metres in length.

The use of U.S.-produced corn ethanol also highlights the increasingly interconnected nature of the energy, agricultural and maritime sectors.

The U.S. is already a major global ethanol producer, with an established network of production facilities and distribution infrastructure. POET, for example, says it produces more than three billion gallons of bioethanol annually across its network of 35 bioprocessing facilities.

text:
Kalpana Pathak Mumbai: Engineering conglomerate Larsen & Toubro is in talks with Japan's Itochu Corporation to sell a minority stake in its wholly-owned clean energy unit.

The Japanese general trading giant is also partnering with L&T Energy GreenTech (LTEGL) to develop and commercialise a 300 kilo tonnes per annum (KTPA) green ammonia project at Kandla in Gujarat. "We are in discussion with Japan's Itochu group for equity participation, in addition to the green ammonia offtake," Subramanian Sarma, deputy managing director and president, L&T told ET. He didn't disclose the size of the stake that Itochu may acquire.

LTEGL had earlier raised equity from its parent through rights issues, including an issue specifically intended for the green ammonia development project at Deendayal Port, formerly Kandla Port. LTEGL is building the project in Kandla on a sizeable land parcel acquired by L&T last year for developing green hydrogen and green ammonia projects.

This April, LTEGL signed a long-term take-or-pay agreement to supply 300,000 tonnes per annum of green ammonia from the proposed facility. Through this partnership with LTEGL, supplies from Kandla are expected to support Itochu's bunkering operations in Singapore and other locations, enabling the early adoption of green ammonia as a next-generation marine fuel and supporting the shipping industry's transition to low-carbon operations.

LTEGL may also evaluate offering minority stakes in its green ammonia projects to other international partners, as it seeks to bring external capital into the business and strengthen the financing of its planned projects, said industry sources. L&T's FY26 annual report identified the 300-KTPA Kandla project as a key part of its energy transition strategy.

The move to onboard international equity partners comes as developers of large green hydrogen and ammonia projects increasingly look to combine project development expertise, long-term offtake agreements, and capital from strategic partners to improve the bankability of projects. L&T is looking at the Kandla project as a strategic export hub for green hydrogen derivatives. The company has been building a clean energy platform spanning green hydrogen, green ammonia and related infrastructure.

text:
LONDON: The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black and Red Seas, as well as environmental topics, were among the key issues discussed when BIMCO’s Maritime Safety & Security Committee (MSSC) and Marine Environment Committee (MEC) met on 30 September and 1 October.

Members considered the implications of regional conflicts, attacks on shipping, drones, mines and navigational disruption. The committees also discussed a broad range of other regulatory, safety and environmental issues affecting the day-to-day operation of ships.

These meetings are an important part of how we represent your interests. Our committees bring together industry expertise to identify practical challenges and help shape BIMCO’s positions in discussions with the IMO, governments and regulators.

Digitalisation was another major theme, including the opportunities it offers for efficiency, compliance and safety, as well as the growing importance of cyber security and supporting seafarers as technology develops.

Members also discussed the safe adoption of alternative fuels, including ammonia, hydrogen and methanol, and future safety frameworks for advanced modular nuclear reactors. The continued discussions on the IMO Net-Zero Framework and revisions to the EU ETS also received significant attention.

Operational and human factors featured prominently, including enclosed-space fatalities, hydrogen sulphide exposure, fatigue, crew welfare, criminalisation and suicide prevention.

On environmental regulation, members considered continuing challenges with ballast water management systems, including challenging water quality, reliability, spare parts and access to service engineers. The proposed legally-binding international convention on biofouling was also discussed, with an emphasis on ensuring that future requirements are practical, science-based and capable of consistent implementation across the global fleet.

Other topics included search and rescue and mixed migration, underwater radiated noise, marine plastics and plastic pellet transportation, and implementation of the Hong Kong Convention on ship recycling.

text:
TOKYO : Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, Ltd. on Friday announced that MOL Ocean Bulk Pte. Ltd. , which operates the MOL Group’s overseas Capesize bulker business, has signed a 25-year contract with Vale International S.A. (a subsidiary of Vale S.A.) to transport iron ore using two vessels. As part of Vale’s Shipping decarbonization strategy, the project will employ the world’s first 210,000-metric-ton ore carriers equipped with a tri-fuel propulsion system that can run on ethanol, methanol, and conventional heavy fuel oil. The vessels are scheduled for delivery in 2030 and will primarily carry out the transoceanic transport of the company’s iron ore.

The vessels are not only equipped with tri-fuel engines but also feature an LNG/ammonia-ready design, enabling the future use of either fuel. In addition, they incorporate a range of energy-saving technologies available for next-generation newbuilding vessels. By providing flexibility in fuel selection according to fuel availability, decarbonization benefits, and economic considerations, the vessels broaden practical options for reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in marine transport.

Ethanol could potentially reduce carbon emissions by up to approximately 90% compared with heavy fuel oil on a full lifecycle basis, from fuel production through consumption (Note 1). In recent years, it has attracted growing attention as a renewable fuel, and its ease of handling is expected to streamline wider adoption in marine fuel applications.

Under its “BLUE ACTION 2035 Phase 2” environmental vision, the MOL Group aims to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 2050. Through the operation of these vessels, the group will move ahead toward achieving its own decarbonization targets while helping reduce Vale’s marine transport-related Scope 3 emissions(Note 2). Furthermore, beyond vessel operations, the MOL Group will work toward the decarbonization of the shipping industry and the realization of sustainable resource transport through collaboration with customers and partners across the entire fuel supply chain for ethanol and methanol, from procurement and supply to bunkering.

title: An urgent appeal to help shape the future IMO Biofouling Convention: BIMCO
description:
LONDON: IMO member states are negotiating what will become the first legally binding global Convention on biofouling management.
Proposals under discussion include mandatory biofouling assessments, cleaning requirements linked to prescribed thresholds, deadlines for corrective action, certification requirements and enforcement measures that could ultimately affect a vessel’s ability to trade internationally.
We want to hear about your experience of inspections, cleaning, coatings, operational constraints, service availability and the practical challenges of managing biofouling.
Previous BIMCO surveys have helped demonstrate the industry’s commitment to biofouling management and identify practical implementation challenges.
If industry does not provide its operational experience now, others will shape the Convention on its behalf.
text:
LONDON: IMO member states are negotiating what will become the first legally binding global Convention on biofouling management. The decisions being made now could affect how ships are operated, inspected, cleaned and maintained for years to come.

The industry therefore needs to make its voice heard, and we need your help now.

Proposals under discussion include mandatory biofouling assessments, cleaning requirements linked to prescribed thresholds, deadlines for corrective action, certification requirements and enforcement measures that could ultimately affect a vessel’s ability to trade internationally.

IMO member states need evidence about what is achievable in practice, the challenges facing crews and operators, the availability of cleaning services, current approaches to biofouling management and the potential unintended consequences of new requirements.

This is why we are asking you to complete our biofouling survey as soon as possible.

Your response will give us real-world evidence that we can use to help inform the discussions at IMO. We want to hear about your experience of inspections, cleaning, coatings, operational constraints, service availability and the practical challenges of managing biofouling.

Previous BIMCO surveys have helped demonstrate the industry’s commitment to biofouling management and identify practical implementation challenges. The more responses we receive, the stronger the evidence we can bring to the negotiations.

Whether you operate one ship or a large fleet, your experience matters. By responding, you can help shape a Convention that is environmentally effective while also being practical, workable and capable of consistent implementation across the global fleet.

If industry does not provide its operational experience now, others will shape the Convention on its behalf.

Please complete the survey as soon as possible and help us ensure the industry’s voice is heard.

text:
India is making further progress in positioning itself as a global leader in the export of alternative fuels in shipping. Ports Minister Sarbananda Sonowal and Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel recently participated in laying the foundation for an e-methanol plant at Deendayal Port Authority (DPA) in Kandla, Gujarat. This is the first port-based e-methanol production facility in India. The project is part of the government’s wider campaign to promote cleaner maritime transport in the country.

The facility is also poised to make India a competitive global supplier of green shipping fuels. The plant is scheduled to produce green methanol at much lower cost compared to other global producers, just $750 per ton, against a global rate of $1,300 per ton.

Recent research has highlighted three Indian ports with strategic advantages to support green fuel production. DPA on India’s west coast is one of the mentioned ports, which is already hosting major investments in green hydrogen production. Last year, the port commissioned L&T Energy to build a 1 MW green hydrogen plant as part of a larger 10MW project.

Again, DPA in April conducted India’s first methanol bunkering demonstration, which at the time was said to be a lead-up activity to the e-methanol plant. With the facility now launched, India’s role in global maritime decarbonization is firming up. The $240 million plant is expected to produce 150 tons per day of e-methanol once fully built. It will use green hydrogen, water, and biogenic CO2 to produce the e-methanol. DPA is targeting to become a major bunkering hub for methanol-powered vessels plying the Asia-Europe trade corridor.

title: Widening Gap On Green Goals | Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide
description:
The report assessed the industry against five levers of change: technology and supply, demand, finance, policy and civil society.
While it found technology and supply and civil society partially on track, demand, finance and policy are not on track.
The result, the report warns, can become self-reinforcing as fears over insufficient fuel supply encourage owners to order conventional fossil-fuelled tonnage.
Green hydrogen costs are also still “substantially above levels needed” to reach the targeted $1.5-$2.0/kg by 2030.
The Poseidon Principles Annual Disclosure Report 2025 recorded its strongest year-on-year improvement in climate alignment since the framework was established.
text:
Shipping is falling behind the trajectory needed to achieve its 2030 green fuel ambitions, with weakening demand, stalled finance and regulatory uncertainty increasingly threatening to undermine strong progress in technology and fuel supply.

That’s the conclusion of the 2026 edition of Climate Action in Shipping: Progress Towards Shipping’s 2030 Breakthrough, a joint report from the UCL Energy Institute and the Getting to Zero Coalition. The report assessed the industry against five levers of change: technology and supply, demand, finance, policy and civil society. While it found technology and supply and civil society partially on track, demand, finance and policy are not on track.

Between 5% and 10% of the fuel consumed by shipping in 2030 needs to comprise scalable zero-emission fuels (SZEF) if the industry is to remain aligned with the International Maritime Organization’s 2023 greenhouse gas strategy. That corresponds to 0.6-1.2 exajoules of energy, approximately 15-30 million tonnes of heavy fuel oil equivalent annually, or enough fuel for around 600-1,200 15,000-TEU container ships, according to the report.

But “overall performance indicators lag behind what is needed”, the report states and in some areas, progress has actually reversed.

Central to that deterioration was the failure to adopt the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF) in October 2025, an outcome the report links to company decisions being paused or cancelled and weakening sentiment across finance and demand.

Make amends

Yet the report stresses that opportunity has not disappeared. Supply and technology continue to progress and it remains feasible to achieve high levels of SZEF production consistent with a pathway towards net zero in 2050. Instead, the greater danger is that shipping lacks sufficient SZEF-capable vessels because regulatory uncertainty discourages investment. The result, the report warns, can become self-reinforcing as fears over insufficient fuel supply encourage owners to order conventional fossil-fuelled tonnage.

Technology provides perhaps the clearest counterpoint to that pessimism. The first sea trials of large ammonia-fuelled vessels equipped with two-stroke engines have been successfully completed, while the first ship-to-ship ammonia bunkering operation has taken place. Everllence, Wärtsilä and WinGD have also announced new methanol retrofit offerings. Meanwhile, the number of ports offering methanol bunkering have increased from 19 to 29.

Fuel production nevertheless remains well short of the required trajectory. Total SZEF production remained below 0.02 EJ in 2025 compared with a breakthrough target of 0.10 EJ. The report now expects that milestone to be surpassed in 2028, while the 0.6 EJ target originally targeted for 2030 is likely to be passed between 2032 and 2035 under its low and medium ramp-up scenarios. Green hydrogen costs are also still “substantially above levels needed” to reach the targeted $1.5-$2.0/kg by 2030.

Demand presents a particularly mixed picture.

The long-awaited delivery of methanol-capable containerships produced the largest annual capability gain recorded by the study. Methanol-capable in-service tonnage more than tripled from 2.3 million to 7.7 million GT, lifting SZEF-capable tonnage from 0.41% to 0.77% of the active fleet.

But the forward orderbook moved sharply in the opposite direction. SZEF-capable vessels fell from 9.5% to 5.7% of GT ordered, with both methanol- and ammonia-compatible ordering declining. The 2024 shift away from conventional fuels therefore looks, according to the report, like “a one-off pulse driven by a few large operators rather than a structural break in ordering behaviour”.

Expected potential SZEF demand in 2030 consequently stands at around 0.45 EJ, equivalent to about 450 large containerships, against roughly 600 needed to reach the lower 5% breakthrough threshold. Re-establishing the pre-2025 growth trajectory for SZEF-capable ordering could raise capacity to 0.70 EJ and clear that threshold, illustrating how much hinges on ordering decisions over the remainder of the decade.

Limited appetite

Cargo owners are providing little encouragement. Their willingness to pay a premium for low-carbon shipping fell from 4.5% to 3%, while the proportion expecting to pay more within five years dropped from 65% to 45%. Despite the number of Getting to Zero Coalition members offering zero-emission shipping services more than doubling from four to nine, the report concludes that demand from cargo owners “is not keeping pace with that growth” and says this further demonstrates that the market alone is unlikely to prompt the required fleet shift.

Finance offers another split picture. The Poseidon Principles Annual Disclosure Report 2025 recorded its strongest year-on-year improvement in climate alignment since the framework was established. Around 29% of global ship finance is now covered by transparent IMO-aligned climate disclosure.

However, sustainable finance entering shipping has plateaued.

Around $3 billion of shipping-specific sustainable debt was issued in 2025, down from $3.4 billion in 2024. One $1.1 billion Hapag-Lloyd green loan accounted for 37% of the year’s shipping issuance, while only 10% was approved by the Climate Bonds Initiative. The report therefore judges finance “partially on track to align shipping portfolios, but not to align the flow of capital”.

Policy is where the report identifies the most damaging reversal. Although the draft NZF was approved in April 2025, its formal adoption failed in October and the extraordinary IMO session was adjourned for one year. While negotiations became more constructive at MEPC 84 in April 2026, substantial uncertainties remain over fuel eligibility, rewards and the system’s implementation architecture. National and regional initiatives in the UK, Singapore and Europe have progressed but are regarded as too uneven and limited to replace global regulatory certainty.

Civil society, meanwhile, remains only partially on track despite advances in workforce standards, alternative-fuel training and participation by climate-vulnerable and Indigenous actors at the IMO. Local campaigning around ports remains especially limited, with active campaigns identified at just eight of the world’s top 50 container ports during 2025.

Against that backdrop, the report places regulation firmly at the top of its prescription for recovery, arguing that the IMO should adopt the NZF “‘as is’ within 2026”. It describes the failure to adopt the framework in October 2025 as “the single most transition-regressive event of the five years this report has been running”.
